721.t: Horn voicings: trumpet, tenor, trombone and unison
721.s: Malone explains standard R&B voicings on an F7 chord and why unison is best for small horn sections.
721.q: Well the mess — no I basically followed the cue of standard rhythm & blues voicings. If you have an F7 chord you have the trumpet on the F at the top, a sixth below you have the tenor on the A, and you have the trombone on the E flat below that. And that’s the standard voicing. And when you have a…

721.t: Horn section sizes, home sessions and Jerry Hey
721.s: Typical horn section setups, recording horns at home and sending them back, and admiration for Jerry Hey's unison writing.
721.q: It depends on the style of music. A typical rock & roll session is trumpet, tenor, trombone, baritone. Now Tower of Power had two trumpets, two tenors, and baritone. And, but that four-piece thing for rhythm & blues and rock & roll is pretty much standard.

721.t: How he approaches an arrangement; the horns as frosting
721.s: He listens first, fills slots around the vocal, and keeps horns out of the singer's way.
721.q: Oh of course. If I have a clue as to what I’m going to do. I usually listen to the music and then all kinds of ideas come into my mind and when I get in front of the computer I just filter through those ideas. But a lot of stuff I do is for rock stuff with vocals on them so basically you either…

146.t: Voicing from the top lead down
146.s: Smith explains building chords from the trumpet lead, second part a fifth below and baritone on the tonic.
146.q: Oh yeah, sure. You could do that. Especially when you got too many horns there and you ain't got nowhere else

146.t: Spreading brass, closing saxophones and flatted fifths
146.s: Smith explains scoring above the lead, placing flatted fifths in the middle, and spacing brass wider than saxophones.
146.q: Flatted fifths? No. It was going with the chords, what effect I wanted to get out of that. Whatever I wanted the chord to sound like. In other words, them flatted fifths and things were mostly going to be in the middle somewhere. Yeah, you've got to put them in the middle.

146.t: Smith preferred arranging to taking solos
146.s: Smith says he liked hearing the horns play arrangements and making a five-piece band sound like seventeen.
146.q: No. All I like... Mostly I didn't care nothin' about being no outstanding...playing a whole lot of solos or nothin' like that. All I would like is to raise(?)... I'd like to hear them horns play the arrangements, and voicing in them different kind of chords ...(? )...

694.t: Writing horn parts and unusual keys
694.s: Hunter picks out harmonies on guitar, gives the baritone the hard unmelodic part, and writes in keys like A flat.
694.q: I do that, yeah. They contribute to it. They’ll add suggestions. But for the most part, it’s fairly easy for me ‘cause I couldn’t just spin most of it out of my own head and just hum it to them and play it, I’m able to pick it out on the guitar, what will harmonize. So if you play an instrument…

694.s: Hunter explains his tenor-baritone pairing, inspired by Guitar Slim and Edgar Blanchard, and how he varies voicings behind the vocal.
694.q: It would be different. I mean the thing is, the reason I initially went for that is cause you could get the most range, or the most variety of sounds between the two. So I went for that initially because a lot of the New Orleans rhythm & blues stuff I was listening to like Guitar Slim, Edgar…

1036.t: Hating microphones on every instrument; write for live balance
1036.s: Larry Wilcox taught him to write for live sound rather than the microphone; he learned arranging from Holman, Wilcox and Mancini, not books.
1036.q: Hate it. I hate it. You know you lose that natural balance of the ensemble. I can see tweaking the piano just a little bit, maybe one mic on the piano. But if you’re going to play to microphones you’re not going to have a normal balance of a big band. There’s — Larry Wilcox, great arranger in New…

1036.t: Coupling flugelhorn with lead alto, borrowed from Thad Jones
1036.s: He took the idea of coupling a trumpet with the saxes from Thad Jones; arrangers all steal from each other.
1036.q: Yeah I stole that from Thad Jones. Yeah Thad would always couple the flugelhorn with the lead alto and/or if the lead melody line in the saxes is a soprano sax, which is a very weak instrument, then he would couple the flugelhorn with the soprano in the melody and

674.t: The written part is a guide, and his horn Bessie
674.s: He realised Ellington's charts were only a guide, criticizes arrangers, and describes his trombone as an extension of himself.
674.q: Music is not paper. Paper is not music. You know what the old guys used to say to me? This is a guide. And I thought ah these old guys are talking such trash, I don’t know if they really mean this is a guide. And I finally got it one day, years later, like playing with Duke or something, when I had…

719.t: Staying out of the vocal; the unison approach
719.s: Horns must not compete with the vocal; Quincy Jones advised blending into the rhythm track; unisons carry a line through heavy harmony.
719.q: Absolutely. That is one hundred percent right. If you’re playing when the vocal is playing the horns are not going to be heard because the vocal has to be heard.

822.t: Inner sax parts and good arranging
822.s: Fourth tenor and second alto parts are not easier; good writers like Phil Kelly cross parts for voice leading.
822.q: Well that’s one thing about good arrangers who actually take the time to, you know like sometimes the second tenor and the fourth tenor cross parts, just for voice leading, just so that you don’t have to play two repeated notes. So all of the sudden the fourth tenor is above the second tenor…

487.t: Why five horns in his ensemble
487.s: His albums use two trumpets, trombone, alto and tenor to get both small-group and big-band feeling; using only two horns behind a soloist.
487.q: That’s a rough question. As you can tell, my own albums used five horns: two trumpets, trombone, alto sax and tenor sax. And the reason I chose that is because I can get a small group feeling and a larger group feeling out of the same instrumentation and there are some spots where even people have…

948.t: Hearing an arrangement sung; arranging for voices and a cappella
948.s: Arrangements on paper need tweaking when sung; pianists must understand breathing; a cappella writing differs.
948.q: Bliss on a stick. Oh yeah. It’s amazing. And over the years of doing a lot of these arrangements, mainly for the Manhattan Transfer, I got to understand that what you put on paper doesn’t necessarily translate to the voices. When you actually hear it being sung there still needs to be tweaking.…

933.t: Learning to write for horns from guitar voicings
933.s: He took theory in high school and wrote for four or five horns at 13-14, using guitar voicings; for two horns he uses the third and seventh.
933.q: Well I always listened – I used to listen to – it was funny, even some of my guitar lines come from horn players. I got most of how I play jazz from listening to horn players. Like I would listen to Lee Morgan for instance like that, I had that record “Sidewinder” you know. And I’d arranged that a…

525.t: Voicing the Cookers and love of three-horn sextet writing
525.s: Weiss explains placing the alto between two trumpets in the Cookers, the eight-horn Wayne Shorter project, and his love of Blue Note and Slide Hampton sextet voicings.
525.q: It’s bright but also I mean the one thing I always found with the Cookers or the Night of the Cookers and stuff like that is voicings. Because you know the tendency, what I do with the Cookers is I always put the — if I can, is put the alto between the two trumpets. Because otherwise, I don’t know,…

982.t: Horn voicings applied to piano comping
982.s: Good voicing works the same on piano as for horns; Thad's brass writing sounds great on piano.
982.q: Absolutely. You know what an arranger does in the big band is orchestrated accompaniment, and at the piano is improvised accompaniment. But they should be just as good. They should both be as good as possible. And what I found is that, not to get too technical here, but a good voicing, a good…

223.t: How he approaches arranging: writing for others, soloists and block voicings
223.s: He writes from an impression of the person he is writing for, wonders about Shorty Rogers's formula, singers' backgrounds, four-part block harmony and Tony Bennett's Basie-style charts.
223.q: As I said before, when I‟m writing for someone else, I have an impression of that person and an impression of his music. I‟m able to use that as a starting point to put in my two cents worth, to elaborate on what they did, to put my own slant on it. I don‟t know if that‟s something I picked up…

328.t: Writing big sound for three horns, learned from Blakey
328.s: Blakey's Jazz Messengers got a big sound from three horns, which shaped his octet writing.
328.q: Yeah, because they were the ones that were writing three horns and accomplishing a big sound. They probably did it because they weren’t that well trained in orchestration. So they just did what they thought would make a good sound. It ended up being that the trumpet was a long ways – a big interval…

227.t: Five- and six-way saxophone voicings and drop twos
227.s: Mandel explains his preference for five- and six-way saxophone voicings, using at least two altos, and compares his usage with Thad Jones's drop-two voicings.
227.ch: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
227.q: I generally favor five way voicing’s, I’m not really one of those four-part harmony with a double-lead writers. I don’t do that a lot, unless I want that particular effect, but that's not I’d say a general working tool for me. I like writing five ways very much, I like writing six ways, I love…

453.t: His arranging style: counterpoint, offbeat voicings and chord colors
453.s: Randolph describes writing in counterpoint rather than concerted style and finding his ahead-of-time harmonies hard to put over.
453.q: Oh, yes, I was arranging then. I was using (unintelligible) characteristic of chords and rhythms that they are really doing (now) I was doing it back then in those times. Because everybody will tell me, you were ahead, and they couldn't -- and I had a hard time getting it through -- getting my work…

91.t: Writing a saxophone chorus: Lonesome Nights
91.s: Patrick describes the four-part block voicings in Lonesome Nights; Carter says music is hard to put in words.
91.q: Well, I think the best way it could be described would be by listening to it! But it's very difficult to put music into words, and that's why -- you know, to show someone a technique of writing, that's something different, but to say how to describe music, I don't know, Jim. I'm not good at…

234.t: Harmony, instrument choice and balance in his arrangements
234.s: Gil says harmony shapes orchestral sound, and explains how he wrote so the parts balanced themselves.
234.q: The harmony gets the sound. A certain way you harmonise things gives the orchestra a certain sound and it adds if there is tension or spite or salt or vinegar or whatever you want to call, or however you want to call it. I don't know what to say about it. I just, I've always, I've always needed it…

170.t: Jack of all trades, and arrangers who do not play
170.s: Ware says most players excel at one instrument and arrangers should know each.
170.q: boils down to individual being motivated, if he really wanted to learn, you know. Like you were speaking a moment ago about having more than one instrument. That reminded me of a certain master --
